title: Chicago Fire's new stadium to be named McDonald's Park
author: Abby Miller
summary: <p>The Chicago Fire's stadium at The 78 has a new moniker — McDonald’s Park — as part of a naming rights deal announced Wednesday.</p><p>“As we take the next step on our journey to build a world class Club, our commitment to Chicago is at the center of everything we do,” Joe Mansueto, the billionaire owner and chairman of the Fire, said in a news release. “That’s why McDonald’s is the perfect partner — an iconic global brand with deep Chicago roots and shared values in supporting our community. McDonald’s Park will be the stadium that Chicago deserves.”</p><p>The deal marks the first time McDonald’s has inked a naming rights partnership for a major professional sports stadium in the U.S., according to a news release. The Chicago-based fast food chain will hold the naming rights until at least 2040. </p><p>The Fire declined to share financial terms of the deal. McDonald’s didn’t respond to a request for comment.</p><p>McDonald’s Park is expected to open in 2028 — in time for the 2028-2029 MLS season, which starts in summer 2028. </p><p>There will be a McDonald’s flagship restaurant, expected to open in spring 2028, and the stadium will host year-round events such as concerts, community events and fan experiences.</p><p>“Together, we are creating more than a stadium,” Chris Kempczinski, chairman and CEO of McDonald’s, said. “We are building a place that serves up joy, brings together community, delivers impact and is designed to serve generations to come.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-fa0000" name="image-fa0000"></a> also have access to pregame meet‑and‑greets and special experiences, according to the Fire.</p><p>Starting next year, McDonald's will be the presenting partner of the <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagofirefc.com/news/chicago-fire-foundation-launches-plays-program" target="_blank" >Fire’s Participate, Learn, Achieve, Youth Soccer</a> program, which offers free soccer programs at Chicago Public Schools. The deal will help expand the P.L.A.Y.S. program’s presence from 70 schools to 140 by the time McDonald’s Park opens. The partners’ long-term vision is to serve more than 280 CPS elementary schools, which would be more than 125,000 students.</p><p>The Fire <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/03/03/chicago-fire-football-club-breaks-ground-650-million-stadium-78" >broke ground</a> on its $750 million South Loop stadium in March. The 22,000-seat stadium, bankrolled by Mansueto, will be a huge boon for the team, which currently plays at Soldier Field but has had games pushed to the suburbs due to scheduling conflicts with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/11/bears-stadium-arlington-heights-hammond-indiana-what-to-know" >Bears</a> and concerts.</p><p>The stadium will serve as an anchor for The 78, the 62-acre site at Roosevelt Road and Clark Street that had eluded development for years. The land was one of the largest undeveloped parcels left in the city.</p><p>The first phase of development at The 78 will include more than 1,400 feet of publicly-accessible riverfront space, a new water taxi stop, 1 1/2 miles of bike trails, Divvy bike stations, two temporary surface parking lots, public parking and 3 acres of sports fields, according to owner Related Midwest.</p><p>Initial stadium renderings show a property that resembles a warehouse, invoking Chicago’s industrial manufacturing roots. The updated renderings, shared Wednesday, now have McDonald’s signature golden arches and company name above the entrance and inside the stadium.</p><p>While it's unclear how much McDonald's paid for naming rights, other companies have doled out millions in similar deals. When the White Sox signed its 13-year deal with Rate, then called Guaranteed Rate, it was estimated to be <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2024/12/17/white-sox-ballpark-has-new-name-rate-field" >$2 million per season</a>.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/03/03/chicago-fire-football-club-breaks-ground-650-million-stadium-78" >Chicago Fire breaks ground on $750 million stadium at The 78</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

title: Arlington Heights or Hammond, Indiana? What to know in the Bears' stadium saga
author: Mitchell Armentrout
summary: <p>A five-year stadium odyssey could finally come to a head this spring for the Chicago Bears.</p><p>The team has secured a sweetheart deal from Indiana lawmakers that would help them build a new dome in Hammond, leaving it up to Illinois legislators to decide on property tax incentives that could at least keep them in their home state, if not their home city.</p><p>Here’s what’s at stake with the political football sitting at the goal line as the clock winds down on the legislative session in Springfield.</p><h3><b>Why do the Bears want to move?</b></h3><p>To make more money. Soldier Field is the smallest stadium in the NFL, and the Bears rent it from the Chicago Park District. Owning a bigger dome would allow the team to sell more tickets and rake in more revenue from concerts and other events.</p><h3><b>Where could the Bears go?</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Arlington Heights or Hammond, Indiana, are the only choices at this point, according to the team. But they’ve waffled on their preferred destination over the past few years.</p><p>The Bears explored <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2023/6/11/23754606/bears-stadium-arlington-heights-naperville-chicago-odds" target="_blank" ><u>a bevy of options</u></a> across the suburbs and made a full-court press for a new lakefront dome near Soldier Field that was soundly rejected by Illinois lawmakers. Then they leaned heavily toward Arlington Heights but, absent legislative support, announced last fall they were seriously considering crossing the state line <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/04/28/chicago-bears-hammond-hams-escalating-rhetoric-hoosiers-hope-bears-stadium" target="_blank" ><u>to Indiana</u></a>.</p><h3><b>But they’re definitely leaving Chicago?</b></h3><p>Yes, barring a sudden change of heart. Mayor Brandon Johnson cheered alongside Bears president Kevin Warren for their lakefront proposal in 2024, but Gov. JB Pritzker and legislative leaders threw cold water on that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2024/04/23/bears-new-stadium-dome-lakefront-soldier-field" target="_blank" ><u>expensive pitch</u></a> before the Bears’ press conference even ended. It would’ve required about $900 million in taxpayer funding and at least as much in other infrastructure spending.</p><p>Cook County Board President Toni Preckwinkle and other local leaders wanted the Bears to build on the old Michael Reese Hospital site in Bronzeville, but the team says it’s too narrow for an NFL stadium, and they haven’t identified any other workable sites within city limits.</p><p>Johnson is still working on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/05/mayor-brandon-johnson-bears-stadium-legislation-arlington-heights-kam-buckner" target="_blank" ><u>a Hail Mary pitch</u></a> to keep the Bears in the city, but he hasn’t built up much Springfield clout in his term.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div A new stadium would take up less than half the site, which they’ve envisioned as a mixed-use development with retail, restaurants and residential areas.</p><p>It’s also closer to their Halas Hall training facility, which the Bears renovated in 2019 at a cost of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/02/20/bears-nfl-halas-hall-practice-facility" target="_blank" ><u>more than $100 million</u></a>. And while Chicago is a Bears town across the board, a huge portion of their fan base lives in the northwest suburbs.</p><h3><b>So why haven’t they built a stadium in Arlington Heights already?</b></h3><p>Their property tax bill would be astronomical. The team already isn’t thrilled with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/bears-stadium/2024/12/12/bears-stadium-arlington-property-tax-deal" target="_blank" ><u>the $3.6 million they’re paying</u></a> annually on the vacant Arlington site, and without a change to state law, they’d easily owe upwards of $150 million in property taxes each year when it’s fully developed.</p><p>That’s why they want Illinois lawmakers to pass so-called<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/04/22/bears-stadium-arlington-heights-property-tax-relief-infrastructure-northwest-indiana" > megaproject legislation</a>, which allows companies to negotiate discounted payments in lieu of taxes (PILOT) with local taxing bodies, saving them hundreds of millions of dollars over the next four decades.</p><div class="Enhancement" 2022.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided by Chicago Bears</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>What’s on the table in Indiana?</b></h3><p>A tantalizing deal for the McCaskey family. Hoosier lawmakers authorized a new stadium authority that could put at least a billion taxpayer dollars into a dome in Hammond, backed by a slew of new taxes on admissions, hotel stays, food and beverages, plus a toll hike.</p><p>The Bears, who have committed to spending $2 billion on stadium construction wherever they end up, would retain all revenue generated by the dome and have the option to buy it for a buck once 40-year bonds are paid off by taxpayers.</p><p>While many Springfield observers view the Indiana threat as a leverage play for the team to get what it wants in Illinois, the bottom line makes it a tempting proposition.</p><h3><b>So why haven’t they left for Indiana already?</b></h3><p>The Bears are still going through their due diligence evaluating the Hammond site at the Lost Marsh Golf Course. It’s built over an old industrial dump within sniffing distance of an oil refinery, and situated near a Superfund site flagged by environmental regulators for toxin-tainted soil.</p><p>Logistical hurdles aside, the team would also face public blowback for leaving behind not only Chicago but the state that has supported a franchise now valued at nearly $9 billion.</p><h3><b>Will the Bears get their megaproject legislation from Springfield?</b></h3><p>That’s the billion-dollar question. The megaproject bill that passed the Illinois House last month marked the first significant legislative win for the team after four fruitless years of lobbying Springfield, but it’ll have to be significantly overhauled to pass the Illinois Senate or become palatable for the Bears. The bill sponsored by state Rep. Kam Buckner, D-Chicago, included a number of late additions without consulting the team, Senate leaders or Pritzker’s office.</p><p>The main sticking point is a provision calling for half of PILOT payments to be directed toward property tax relief for average homeowners. The governor’s office says that relief would be <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/04/bears-stadium-property-tax-relief-pritzker-negligible" target="_blank" ><u>negligible</u></a>, and from the Bears’ perspective, it would wipe out much of their potential PILOT savings.</p><p>State Sen. Bill Cunningham, the South Side Democrat leading talks in his chamber, said he’s optimistic they’ll find common ground in the next few weeks.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-820000" name="image-820000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7711221/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6569x3687+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F04%2F1c%2F144a7e8c40758df794cac3cb76d0%2Fmasstransit-121725-008.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3d7e6a7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6569x3687+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F04%2F1c%2F144a7e8c40758df794cac3cb76d0%2Fmasstransit-121725-008.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/343f2c8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6569x3687+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F04%2F1c%2F144a7e8c40758df794cac3cb76d0%2Fmasstransit-121725-008.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Governor JB Pritzker (left) stands with Senate President Don Harmon (center) and House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch (right) during the signing ceremony for the Northern Illinois Transit Authority Act at Union Station in The Loop, Tuesday, Dec. 16, 2025. JB Pritzker (left) stands with Senate President Don Harmon (center) and House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch (right) during the signing ceremony for the Northern Illinois Transit Authority Act at Union Station in The Loop, Tuesday, Dec. 16, 2025. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>What are the political stakes?</b></h3><p>No Chicago legislator wants to be held responsible for letting the team leave the city. That’s also true for progressives, though they are wary of giving any help to a multi-billion dollar corporation while everyday costs rise for average residents. </p><p>Pritzker doesn’t want to be remembered as the governor who lost the Bears, and while he’s long pushed for megaproject incentives, he also doesn’t want to be viewed as securing a handout for a lucrative pro sports franchise.</p><p>Nor does Johnson want to go down as the mayor who lost the Bears, although he can pin much of the blame on his predecessor, Lori Lightfoot. The question for Johnson is whether his effort <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/05/mayor-brandon-johnson-bears-stadium-legislation-arlington-heights-kam-buckner" target="_blank" ><u>to tank the Arlington Heights deal</u></a> is worth pushing the Bears across the border.</p><h3><b>What will it cost taxpayers?</b></h3><p>Indiana taxpayers would be on the hook for a whole suite of new taxes to build the Bears a stadium, but it’s harder to pin down the full cost for Illinoisans.</p><p>An estimated $855 million in public dollars would be needed to install sewers, water mains, traffic upgrades and other infrastructure <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2025/10/01/bears-stadium-arlington-heights-cost-renderings" target="_blank" ><u>to support the Arlington Heights development</u></a>. But a lot of those projects have already been earmarked and will be done regardless of whether a dome gets built, Pritzker has argued.</p><p>Beyond that, megaproject legislation would save the Bears hundreds of millions of dollars that would otherwise be going to local school districts and other taxing bodies. But the officials from the team — and other big businesses that might be incentivized to make big investments and create jobs — are quick to point out the schools are missing out on even more money without big projects raising property values.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-8d0000" name="image-8d0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/41c3b70/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6117x3433+0+323/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5f%2F79%2Fe09a68e84fb3a6caf03f0ae3decf%2Fbears-260111-91-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/521a5fd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6117x3433+0+323/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5f%2F79%2Fe09a68e84fb3a6caf03f0ae3decf%2Fbears-260111-91-1.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/53331a6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6117x3433+0+323/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5f%2F79%2Fe09a68e84fb3a6caf03f0ae3decf%2Fbears-260111-91-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Chicago Bears cornerback Nahshon Wright #26 hypes up the crowd after warm-ups before the Bears take on the Green Bay Packers in an NFC wild-card game at Soldier Field, Saturday, Jan. 10, 2026. </div><p></p><h3><b>What will happen to Soldier Field?</b></h3><p>The Chicago Fire will play at Soldier Field until their new, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/03/03/chicago-fire-football-club-breaks-ground-650-million-stadium-78" target="_blank" ><u>privately funded stadium</u></a> is finished in the South Loop in 2028.</p><p>Soldier Field is still the city’s premier summer concert venue, and Johnson’s administration is looking <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/02/24/soldier-field-renovation-post-chicago-bears-era-illinois-general-assembly" target="_blank" ><u>to secure $630 million from the state</u></a> for renovations to keep it viable even without 10 or so Bears games on the calendar.</p><p>Taxpayers are still footing the bill for the field’s 2003 renovation, with some $467 million in bonds still outstanding.</p><h3><b>When will the Bears make a decision?</b></h3><p>Soon ... probably. Warren has said they’ll name their destination in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/04/01/bears-president-kevin-warren-targets-late-spring-or-early-summer-for-stadium-decision" target="_blank" ><u>late spring or early summer</u></a>. That’s coming from the executive who previously said he wanted shovels in the ground by the end of 2024, and again in ‘25.</p><p>But with Indiana’s offer in hand — and under pressure from the NFL to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/04/29/bears-meet-with-nfl-committee-stadium-and-plan-to-do-so-again-in-may" >pick a lane</a> — the stadium saga finally appears to be nearing a climax. The team won’t make any announcement until after they see what they get from Illinois lawmakers, whose spring session concludes May 31.</p><p>Bills can still move in Springfield after that date, but with a higher threshold for passage that would suggest season-ticket holders should start mapping out their Indiana commutes.</p>

title: Mayor Johnson determined to block Bears' move to Arlington Heights
author: Fran Spielman
summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson on Tuesday mounted the legislative equivalent of a goal line stand against the Bears’ quest for the property tax break needed to pave the way for a domed stadium in Arlington Heights.</p><p>Johnson questioned why any lawmaker from Chicago would even think about providing a massive tax break for a professional sports team valued at nearly $9 billion, while ignoring the need for what he calls progressive revenue to increase school funding and help working people struggling to make ends meet.</p><p>“If we’re asking anyone to tighten the belt, we should look at whose belt is exploding — and that’s the ultra-rich. As their bellies get fat and our people are starving, this is not the time to balance the budget off the backs of working people,” the mayor said at his weekly news conference.</p><p>“The type of tax structure that they would set up for large corporations and billionaires without a clear pathway to provide certainty as well as equity for everyday working people, I believe that’s a mismatch there. And quite frankly, the infrastructure they’re even discussing in the suburbs — those infrastructure needs have been present on the lakefront for a very long time.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/04/22/bears-stadium-arlington-heights-property-tax-relief-infrastructure-northwest-indiana" >Bears exit from Chicago closer to reality as House passes bill helping Arlington Heights bid</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Hours before joining fellow Chicago area mayors in Springfield, where he has had little success, Johnson made it clear that he would use whatever political muscle he has to block the so-called <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/04/bears-stadium-property-tax-relief-pritzker-negligible" >megaprojects bill</a> now before the Illinois Senate after clearing the Illinois House April 22.</p><p>Though Chicago is no longer part of the conversation to build a domed stadium needed to keep the Bears in Illinois and stave off a move to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/04/28/chicago-bears-hammond-hams-escalating-rhetoric-hoosiers-hope-bears-stadium" >Northwest Indiana,</a> Johnson is still holding out hope to keep the Bears in the city.</p><p>“I’m building things in this city. I want to build more things in this city. Why is that important? Because it creates opportunities for Chicagoans,” Johnson said. “Why would I advocate for something that wouldn’t benefit the people of Chicago? I don’t know why any Chicago legislator would vote for anything that doesn’t benefit the people that they represent.”</p><p> Black contractors need opportunities provided by new construction projects after historically being “shut out,” Johnson said.</p><p>“Arlington Heights? Anywhere else? A Chicagoan having to commute two hours out of their way for a job? That is not something that … anybody who represents Chicago should want,“ Johnson said. “At a time in which property values are increasing and affordability is becoming that much more of a challenge, to do anything in favor of entities with means without supporting families who have needs — I would find that shortsighted.”</p><p>State Rep. Kam Buckner, D-Chicago, countered that the megaprojects bill he stewarded through through the Illinois House with support from 33 members of the Chicago delegation is “replete with tools that help Chicago compete and bring in large-scale developments.”</p><p>“We do it in a way that’s smart and benefits residents,” Buckner told the Chicago Sun-Times. “There are minority contracting requirements in there. There is property tax relief in there for the people of Chicago. There’s jobs. There’s investment. There’s real pathways. Focusing on Arlington Heights is missing the broader conversation about what is in this bill.”</p><p>A “vast majority” of the Chicago delegation “understood that, and you can tell it by the vote,” Buckner said.</p><p>Two years ago, Johnson joined Bears president Kevin Warren in unveiling plans for a domed lakefront stadium adjacent to Soldier Field that would have required $2.4 billion in public support.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/04/24/bears-stadium-bill-jb-pritzker-illinois-senate" >Gov. JB Pritzker </a>and Democratic legislative leaders were conspicuously absent. The mayor’s plan went nowhere in Springfield.</p><p>On Tuesday, Johnson said he has other stadium sites and ideas to keep the Bears in Chicago.</p><p>He refused to reveal specifics. Alternatives include: The 78, site of the new Chicago Fire stadium under construction; the Amtrak site near The 78 eyed by the White Sox for a new ballpark; the stalled One Central megaproject on railyard land near Soldier Field, or the 49-acre Michael Reese Hospital site that the Bears have rejected as too narrow.</p><p>Chicago Park District Supt. Carlos Ramirez-Rosa is preparing for life without the Bears by continuing to lobby for $630 million to renovate Soldier Field and ease the traffic bottleneck that makes it difficult to get in and out of the Museum Campus.</p><p>But Johnson is not giving up hope, even though Arlington Heights and Hammond, Indiana, were the only Bears stadium sites discussed with NFL owners recently.</p><p>On Tuesday, Johnson said he and Ramirez-Rosa agree on the need to improve lakefront access.</p><p>"The campus needs a makeover," Johnson said. "The ingress-egress is absolutely horrific. I don't mean to trigger Bears fans or concertgoers. [But] it is just brutal getting in and out of that space. ... It disrupts the type of flow that would naturally carry over to the rest of the campus," Johnson said.</p><p> </p>

title: UChicago students propose solutions to city's sports stadium conundrum
author: Abby Miller
summary: <p>From Springfield to Indianapolis, the debate over sports facilities is reaching a fever pitch as lawmakers vie for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" >Bears</a> to build a new stadium in their backyard.</p><p>Similar conversations were had last week in Hyde Park as students at the University of Chicago’s Harris School of Public Policy gave their final pitches in the Harris Policy Innovation Challenge — tackling the issue of stadium policy in Chicago.</p><p>The annual contest, launched in 2023, pushes students to find solutions to some of Chicago’s most pressing public policy issues. Finalists are selected to present at a live pitch event, “Shark Tank”-style, and the winning team receives $10,000.</p><p>This year, students were asked what Chicago’s official policy for supporting professional sports teams and facilities should be.</p><p>Winners Charlie Schraw, Christina Tsai and Liz Williams presented judges with a three-pronged approach: create a new stadium securitization corporation, require a community benefits agreement for stadium developments and enforce sustainability standards.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" </figure> </div> </div><p>The stadium securitization corporation is modeled after Chicago’s Sales Tax Securitization Corp., which was established in 2017.</p><p>The stadium corporation would issue bonds strictly for developing the public infrastructure necessary for stadiums, according to the team’s presentation. It would serve as a bankruptcy-remote entity that separates stadium liabilities from the city’s general credit, according to the team.</p><p>Those funds would be lockboxed, meaning restricted to the corporation, resulting in lower interest rates on corporation debt, ultimately leading to declining stadium debt, Tsai said.</p><p></p><p>“The SSC provides a cost-saving framework for funding public infrastructure that's necessary for these stadium deals,” Tsai said during the event. “Having a plan in place allows the city to come to the negotiating table with discipline and leverage — not desperation — and this leverage is what allows the city to negotiate better deals for Chicagoans.”</p><p>Reforming the city’s community benefits agreement process was also important for the team, whose presentation was titled “Structuring the Deal.” The team argued their process, which would require a signed CBA before city bonds are issued, would prioritize Chicagoans in stadium deals.</p><p>Schraw said the team’s CBA model came from looking at projects in Chicago and beyond, including the Obama Presidential Center and the new Highmark Stadium for the Buffalo Bills. Those agreements require minority- and women-owned businesses to be involved in construction, in addition to hiring locally.</p><p>“Something that made our proposal really strong is that we had these considerations that oftentimes are seen as aspirational, in terms of community impact and sustainability, but within our proposal, these actually have teeth,” Williams said. “What really drove us to that is … this tension between the fans and the teams themselves. The fans love these teams, but what are they getting back from them? And we wanted to ensure that that relationship was truly a two-way street.”</p><p>Paired with the CBA are additional sustainability requirements that must be met for the stadium securitization corporation bonds to be issued. Stadiums must align with the city’s Climate Action Plan and produce annual public reports on their energy, water and waste for the duration of the lease. If the stadium is part of a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/04/22/bears-stadium-arlington-heights-property-tax-relief-infrastructure-northwest-indiana" >megadevelopment</a>, the requirements would include the entire project — not just the sports arena.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/04/24/bears-stadium-bill-jb-pritzker-illinois-senate" >Gov. JB Pritzker feels ‘need for speed’ — and changes — with Bears stadium bill</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Williams said while her team’s proposal may slow down negotiations or push teams away, it includes important factors for both the long-term use of stadiums and Chicago’s reputation as a sports city.</p><p>“This framework is for all leagues. When we imagine the Bears, we are also trying to imagine small women's sports leagues. We're also trying to imagine leagues that would grow over time. We're trying to imagine expansion, and that this would then apply to teams both big and small,” Williams said. “We really hope that this plan, these conditions and our enforcement mechanisms ensure that teams ... would actually take care of [fans] and pay them back. We would hope that a team like the Bears and the love that Chicago has for them would recognize that, and all of these conditions are just to improve the community, the durability and the accessibility of their stadium.”</p><p>Other proposals included instituting public referendums to trigger public stadium subsidies and a long-term restructuring of Soldier Field’s ownership structure and requiring sports teams to sell a small, minority equity stake to the city through a new Chicago Sports Authority.</p><p>Justin Marlowe, research professor at the University of Chicago and director of the Center for Municipal Finance, noticed a theme of rethinking stadium governance structure among the three finalists.</p><p>“I think for many people that's the issue: It's seen as this black box ... as something that’s sort of negotiated behind closed doors,” Marlowe said. “What this proposal does … is really center the community in that discussion. What [the winners] did in particular was deliberately blur the lines between community and fans, and essentially make the case to teams that, in fact, it's in your interest to be accommodating to the community and mindful of the community's needs because that's what sustainability for a fan base means in the long run.”</p>

title: Bears meet with NFL stadium committee — and plan to do so again in May
author: Patrick Finley
summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href=" https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> held a virtual meeting with the NFL’s Stadium Committee on Wednesday to provide updates on their potential sites in both Arlington Heights and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/04/28/chicago-bears-hammond-hams-escalating-rhetoric-hoosiers-hope-bears-stadium" target="_blank" >Hammond, Indiana</a> — and plan to meet again virtually in another two weeks or so, a source told the Sun-Times.</p><p>The only two stadium sites up for consideration are the 326 acres the team owns in Arlington Heights and the plot near Wolf Lake in Hammond.</p><p>The Bears also figure to give a stadium update at the NFL’s quarterly meeting May 19-20 in Orlando, though it’s unclear if they will have decided between the two sites by then. The team is preaching urgency in Springfield, where the House passed property tax legislation last week. The legislation must now pass the Senate, and the Bears want key revisions. The Senate adjourns May 31.</p><p>The quarterly meeting features owners from each team. Approval from league ownership — whether it occurs in May or at a later meeting — is part of the NFL’s G-5 funding program, which allows teams to borrow up to $250 million for stadium construction.</p><p>Vikings owner Mark Wilf chairs the stadium committee, which features, among other executives, Bears chairman George McCaskey.</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module title: Chicago Bears or 'Hammond Hams'? Amid escalating rhetoric, Hoosiers hold out hope for new stadium
author: Michael Puente
summary: <p>In the tug-of-war between Illinois and Indiana over the Chicago Bears, Gov. JB Pritzker, who is widely believed to be running for president in 2028, may have already lost a supporter from his own party.</p><p>“I'm not voting for him for president. I can tell you that,” Hammond Mayor Tom McDermott Jr., a Democrat in this blue-collar city, told the Chicago Sun-Times Tuesday.</p><p>McDermott took issue with a <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/watch/?v=1324622733063055" target="_blank" ><u>quip by Pritzker</u></a> in which he jokingly told CNN that “Fans will be very upset if the Bears move across the border and become, I don’t know, the Hammond Hams.”</p><p>“I've always been a fan of JB Pritzker. Obviously he feels very threatened,” McDermott said. “Indiana is a better state to do business in, which is a fact. Obviously he takes issue with that, and then he wants to disparage the city of Hammond.”</p><p>McDermott said the city and state — led by Republican Gov. Mike Braun — are monitoring Illinois’ lawmakers next move to keep the Bears in Illinois.</p><p>Last week, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/04/22/bears-stadium-arlington-heights-property-tax-relief-infrastructure-northwest-indiana" target="_blank" ><u>Illinois House voted</u></a> 78-32 to approve a megaprojects proposal intended to support a new domed stadium on the site of the former Arlington Heights racetrack. The bill represents the first major legislative step toward ensuring the Bears stay in Illinois and fending off an incentive-packed offered by Indiana lawmakers. The Illinois Senate must still approve the measure by the end of next month.</p><p>Pritzker is urging lawmakers to move faster.</p><p>“There is a need for speed here,” Pritzker said last week. “We need to move somewhat expeditiously.”</p><p>But McDermott argues that Indiana’s plan, which includes $1 billion in public funding, is an overall better deal for the Bears.</p><p>“The Bears will save billions of dollars by relocating to Hammond. I feel secure we've done everything that we could possibly do to bring over a world-class organization like the Chicago Bears,” McDermott said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div title: Game plan for Bears stadium bill still in play
author: Rich Miller
summary: <p>“We're almost there” on a Bears stadium bill, Rep. Kam Buckner, D-Chicago, told some sports radio hosts on a Friday morning before the House returned to Springfield for three days of session last week. “We're very close.”</p><p>Asked if the rumor spread by sports business pundit Marc Ganis earlier that week was true about House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch holding up the Bears bill, Buckner, the House's point person on the state megaprojects bill that includes the Arlington Heights Bears stadium complex, flatly denied it.</p><p>“I want to be very unequivocal and clear about this: Nothing can be further from the truth,” Buckner said on WSCR Radio. Welch, he said, “has given me the green light as his representative in these conversations to bring this home, and we're doing that.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bc0000" name="module-bc0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>Buckner accused Ganis, who is widely quoted in sports media on NFL stadium plans, of “a willful mischaracterization. It's a bad faith interpretation of the facts. It's not analysis. It's fabrication with confidence. … It's a convenient fiction dressed up as expertise. It's not helpful, and it's not true.”</p><p>Ouch.</p><p>A few days later, Buckner told the Chicago Sun-Times that he was working on a property tax relief mechanism within the megaprojects bill, but wasn't sure what form it would take.</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker's top staff seemed taken by surprise. An agreement had been made not to alter the deal that had already been cut with the Bears. The object was to figure out a way to attract enough votes to get it to the Senate and reassure the Bears that things were on track.</p><p>The next day, I was able to obtain an advance copy of Buckner's bill and posted it on my website, CapitolFax.com. While Buckner had told reporters that he'd been working "lockstep" with the governor's top staff, Pritzker's office released a terse statement saying, "The Governor’s Office is currently reviewing the draft amendment provided by Capitol Fax and does not have comment at this time."</p><p>The new property tax component would take half of the money that the Bears or other megaproject developers would pay in lieu of property taxes, give some to area local governments for property tax rebates, and then give the rest to the state's property tax relief fund.</p><p>But that would mean the Bears' payment might have to be doubled, because Arlington Heights-area schools and other local governments would see their negotiated payment cut in half. A top source close to Arlington Heights schools said that if the Bears had to pay $400 million instead of $200 million, "That's a Bears problem," not theirs.</p><p>And despite some comments made last week, it really wouldn't produce significant statewide property tax relief. Two years ago, Illinoisans paid $40 billion in property taxes.</p><p>A proposed state constitutional amendment to levy a 3% surcharge on annual personal income over a million dollars, would've thrown big bucks at schools and provided a significant amount for property tax relief. But moderate Democrats and some others refused to support it, and the proposal went nowhere.</p><p>The Senate Democrats were also not made aware of the House's changes in advance, and they weren't happy about it.</p><p>And then there was another problem. The House bill would impose a 9% entertainment tax on the area surrounding the future stadium. Everything from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2024/11/29/pickleball-fastest-growing-sport-chicago-players-indoor-courts" >pickleball </a>to pinball to zip line courses and music venues would be taxed.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/04/24/bears-stadium-bill-jb-pritzker-illinois-senate" >Pritzker</a> told reporters Friday that the amusement tax was something the Bears “were hoping not to see in a bill like this” from the very outset. The Bears would only say that “essential” changes needed to be made to the bill in the Senate.</p><p>Whatever the case, Buckner was able to do what he set out to do: Find enough votes to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/04/22/bears-stadium-arlington-heights-property-tax-relief-infrastructure-northwest-indiana" >pass a bill </a>through the House.</p><p>Buckner’s proposal— <a class="Link" href="https://ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=910&GAID=18&DocTypeID=HB&LegId=156588&SessionID=114" target="_blank" >House Bill 910</a> — received 78 votes, including nine Republicans. Speaker Welch was downright jubilant during a resulting news conference, perhaps relishing his ability to prove doubters and others like Ganis wrong.</p><p>“It's a good night for people all over the state of Illinois because House Democrats deliver,” Welch said. “House Democrats did the work. They believed in the mantra ‘Winners do the work.’ And I want to tell you, we did the work.”</p><p>But there’s still a lot of work to do in the Senate. And then it has to come back to the House after changes are made.</p><p><i>Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ef0000" name="module-ef0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

title: Gov. JB Pritzker feels ‘need for speed’ — and changes — with Bears stadium bill
author: Mitchell Armentrout
summary: <p>Property tax incentive legislation approved by the Illinois House this week needs serious changes to keep the Chicago Bears from jumping the border to Indiana, and state senators need to move quickly to keep that from happening, Gov. JB Pritzker urged on Friday.</p><p>The massive bill sponsored by state Rep. Kam Buckner, D-Chicago, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/04/22/bears-stadium-arlington-heights-property-tax-relief-infrastructure-northwest-indiana" target="_blank" ><u>advanced with bipartisan House support</u></a>, but not in consultation with Pritzker’s office, Senate leaders or even the Bears on some key revisions.</p><p>That leaves the ball on the Senate’s side of the field as the clock winds down toward the legislative deadline of May 31.</p><p>“There is a need for speed here,” Pritzker said after an unrelated news conference at Northwestern University. “We need to move somewhat expeditiously. I realize the Senate has some work to do, and there will be amendments, no doubt about it.”</p><p>While the Bears are due to update the NFL’s stadium committee next week on the status of their yearslong stadium saga, Pritzker predicted the meeting wouldn’t “completely flip the script” in favor of Indiana.</p><p>“Having said that, if there is not true progress that gets made, if it isn't obvious to people that the Senate is moving in the right direction, I think that will make it challenging. But we're all working together,” Pritzker said.</p><p>“I think the Bears want to be in Illinois. I think that's really what their choice would be, if we can put a bill forward that makes sense,” he said. “We just have to make sure that it works for the Bears as it does for the citizens, the residents of the state of Illinois.”</p><p>The so-called megaprojects bill would allow for developers of large projects — like the stadium the Bears have long coveted for Arlington Heights — to negotiate discounted payments in lieu of full property tax bills with local taxing bodies, saving hundreds of millions of dollars over four decades.</p><p>Buckner and other Chicago Democrats have long balked not only at ushering the Bears out of the city, but at handing tax breaks to a franchise valued at nearly $9 billion while homeowners statewide struggle to keep up with their property tax bills.</p><p>Then Indiana lawmakers passed a slew of taxes to help <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/04/17/bears-hammond-indiana-stadium-stadium-site-meeting-kevin-warren-george-mccaskey-thomas-mcdermott-nfl-roger-goodell" target="_blank" ><u>build a stadium in Hammond</u></a> in hopes of luring them east, putting <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/01/16/chicago-bears-stadium-northwest-indiana-arlington-heights-jb-pritzker-kam-buckner" target="_blank" ><u>pressure</u></a> on Illinois legislators to keep them within state borders, if not city limits. The team has all but ruled out a future in Chicago.</p><p>The Illinois House bill that passed 78-32 calls for half the proceeds from payments in lieu of taxes (PILOT) to be set aside for property tax rebates.</p><p>The Bears issued a tepid statement hailing “progress made” in Illinois’ first major legislative step toward a stadium bill, but noted “additional amendments are necessary” to make Arlington Heights a feasible destination.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ed0000" potential PILOT discounts would shrink with half the proceeds diverted to property tax relief funds.</p><p>The only Bears squabble that Pritzker would highlight is a 9% amusement tax.</p><p>“They had said at the outset that an amusement tax is something that really won't work, and that they really don't want to see happen on top of all the other taxes that are imposed here,” Pritzker said. “So we'll see what can happen in the Senate about that.”</p><p>The bill also includes property tax incentives for the “redevelopment of blighted or underused rail yards,” potentially opening the door to a stadium at the South Loop Amtrak yard being eyed by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/18/justin-ishbia-stadium-white-sox-the-78-amtrak" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox across the street from Soldier Field.</p><p>Those are just a few of the provisions in a <a class="Link" href="https://ilga.gov/documents/legislation/104/HB/10400HB0910eng.htm" target="_blank" ><u>375-page bill</u></a> that Pritzker suggested needs to be narrowed down, though he has long emphasized PILOT legislation could attract other big developments.</p><p>“This bill wasn't about the Chicago Bears alone. This bill is really about economic development broadly for the state,” Pritzker said.</p><p>Separate legislation awaits on the $800 million-plus in public funding the team is seeking for sewers, water mains and other infrastructure around the Arlington Heights site, some of them projects that were already earmarked in state plans regardless of the Bears’ ambitions, Pritzker has said.</p><p>The team has committed to spending <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2025/10/01/bears-stadium-arlington-heights-cost-renderings" target="_blank" ><u>$2 billion on the project</u></a>, without any public money for construction of the stadium itself.</p><p>The Illinois Senate gavels back in Tuesday.</p>

>Indie rockers Ratboys evolve from ‘country mouse’ to ‘city rat’ on latest album</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wiujdhl-l-ju/" target="_blank" >Selena Fragassi</a></h5><p>In other rat-related coverage, one of the most solid bands in the city's indie music scene, Ratboys, are in the midst of a banner run.</p><p>The quartet’s sixth record, "Singin’ to an Empty Chair," released Feb. 6, comprises 11 tracks drenched in twangy folk, pop-rock and distortion, and all beating with Midwestern heart. </p><p>It’s a similar vibe to 2023’s "The Window," which helped put the band on the map and led to their first headlining tour across the country; <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wiujdhl-l-tl/" target="_blank" >a Lollapalooza debut</a> a couple years later, not long after singer/guitarist Julia Steiner worked on the festival’s artist transport team; and an appearance on "CBS Saturday Sessions."</p><p>Ten years after forming at the University of Notre Dame, the band is going strong, having just wrapped a national tour and gearing up to play in Europe starting next month.</p><p>But Chicago is still home for Steiner, bassist Sean Neumann and drummer Marcus Nuccio.</p><p>"In Chicago, we all lift each other up. It feels very inclusive … and it’s been that way for a long time," Nuccio said of the city's music scene.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wiujdhl-l-tr/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition!<br>Got a story you think we missed? <a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email us here.</a></p><hr><p><b>Written and curated by</b>: Matt Moore<br><b>Editor</b>: Eydie Cubarrubia</p><hr><p><i>The Chicago Sun-Times is a nonprofit supported by readers like you. title: Lawmakers sweeten pot to keep Bears in Illinois, with stadium bill linked to statewide property tax relief
author: Tina Sfondeles
summary: <p>Illinois hopes to take the lead over Indiana in the Chicago Bears stadium battle with a new proposal that would give the NFL team property tax certainty while also providing a statewide property tax relief sweetener.</p><p>State Rep. Kam Buckner, D-Chicago, plans to brief Illinois House Democrats on the new amendment Tuesday. The PILOT measure, shorthand for payment in lieu of taxes, would allow the Bears to renegotiate their property taxes with Arlington Heights. The property tax relief element, a new addition to stadium-related legislation in Springfield, is essential in getting support from lawmakers outside of Chicago, including Republicans.</p><p>Buckner told the Chicago Sun-Times he would push for lawmakers to hold a committee hearing on the measure and get the proposal to the floor this week as soon as possible, depending on how much support, or resistance, he hears in the caucus.</p><p>“It’ll do something that the state has not done, that other states have not done in megaprojects legislation. It’ll actually consider how these things should be able to help regular taxpayers as well,” Buckner said. "I’m finding a way to bake [in] some property tax relief for homeowners across the state.”</p><p>Buckner said the measure will look at what a special incentive payment looks like for communities, and how a portion of that must go to property tax relief efforts, “both for folks affected in the immediate area, and for folks around the state.”</p><p>“To me, it has to be more than a token,” Buckner said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/02/19/chicago-bears-stadium-hammond-indiana-move" >Hammond Bears? Team says Indiana site near Wolf Lake is now its main stadium focus</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Asked whether the property tax element would help homes or businesses, Buckner acknowledged details were still being worked out but said it would include “definitely a break for homeowners.”</p><p>“It may look like a rebate. It may look like a circuit breaker piece. It may look like money up front on property taxes," Buckner said. “I’m literally working on the fine points of it as we speak, and trying to put together the best version of it.”</p><p>Much of the resistance from Chicago Democrats comes from questions about what will happen to Soldier Field — and how the city will deal with the loss of revenue from the team leaving Chicago. Buckner called Soldier Field concerns “part two” of the discussion. First he has to get the property tax assurance for the Bears squared away for an Arlington Heights domed stadium.</p><p>“This bill is not a Soldier Field bill,” Buckner said. “This is a statewide megaproject mechanism. … This bill will have some things in it that will be helpful for Chicago, particularly because these are things that will be helpful for municipalities across the state. But I don’t think we’ve finished the conversation yet about Soldier Field. We’re still working through that.”</p><p>The property tax piece is an essential first step to move the Bears forward in their Arlington Heights plans. Then lawmakers would take up the infrastructure piece, “and something has to be attached to that about Chicago,” Buckner said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-bb0000" name="image-bb0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/316372b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5603x3145+0+295/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fce%2F3c%2Fa645752f443e8230f3d03a8489ec%2Fforum-021223-22.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2420db0/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5603x3145+0+295/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fce%2F3c%2Fa645752f443e8230f3d03a8489ec%2Fforum-021223-22.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b808582/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5603x3145+0+295/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fce%2F3c%2Fa645752f443e8230f3d03a8489ec%2Fforum-021223-22.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="State Rep. Kam Buckner." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b808582/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5603x3145+0+295/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fce%2F3c%2Fa645752f443e8230f3d03a8489ec%2Fforum-021223-22.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/70f9cc8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5603x3145+0+295/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fce%2F3c%2Fa645752f443e8230f3d03a8489ec%2Fforum-021223-22.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b808582/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5603x3145+0+295/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fce%2F3c%2Fa645752f443e8230f3d03a8489ec%2Fforum-021223-22.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>State Rep. Kam Buckner, a Chicago Democrat, is pushing statewide property tax relief as a sweetener in ongoing talks about legislation aimed at facilitating the Bears’ bid to build a stadium in Arlington Heights.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Buckner said he is confident there are enough votes to clear the first part of the puzzle.</p><p>“You won’t see this bill on the board if the votes were not there,” he said.</p><p>There is pressure building from the NFL — and Gov. JB Pritzker — to get a deal done as soon as possible, especially with Indiana lawmakers nipping at Illinois lawmakers’ heels with its own proposed stadium.</p><p>Chicago Democrats are unlikely to support a measure without other assurances, including discussion of a<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/02/24/soldier-field-renovation-post-chicago-bears-era-illinois-general-assembly" > $630 million ask</a> from the Chicago Park District to renovate and refresh Soldier Field and ease the transportation bottleneck that makes it difficult to get in and out of the Museum Campus.</p><p>“I think the Chicago Dems have to find reasons to support it, and I don’t think we know enough to say that we are going to support it,” Rep. La Shawn Ford, D-Chicago, said. “But as it is, I think Chicago Dems have lots of questions as to, ‘Why should we?’ We’re looking for benefits for Chicago. It’s going to be all about how does it benefit Chicago, and will there be a loss in Chicago?”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> chairman <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/04/01/bears-owner-george-mccaskey-legacy-tradition-wont-stop-potential-move-to-indiana-stadium" target="_blank" >George McCaskey</a> and president/CEO Kevin Warren <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/04/17/bears-hammond-indiana-stadium-stadium-site-meeting-kevin-warren-george-mccaskey-thomas-mcdermott-nfl-roger-goodell" target="_blank" >met with Hammond Mayor Thomas McDermott Jr.</a>, Friday on the site of the team’s proposed Northwest Indiana stadium. The team characterized the gathering as the latest step in due diligence while considering a move across the border to Indiana.</p><p>The meeting took place at the Lost Marsh Golf Club near Wolf Lake, where the Bears would build if they decide to move to Indiana.</p><p>The Bears expect to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/04/01/bears-president-kevin-warren-targets-late-spring-or-early-summer-for-stadium-decision" >make a decision </a>by late spring or early summer.</p><p><i>Contributing: Patrick Finley</i> </p>

title: Bears bosses and Hammond mayor meet on proposed stadium site
author: Patrick Finley
summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> chairman <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/04/01/bears-owner-george-mccaskey-legacy-tradition-wont-stop-potential-move-to-indiana-stadium" target="_blank" >George McCaskey</a> and president/CEO Kevin Warren met with Hammond Mayor Thomas McDermott Jr., Friday on the site of the team's proposed stadium. The team characterized the gathering as the latest step in due diligence while considering a move across the border to Indiana.</p><p></p><p>The meeting, which included other Bears and Hammond officials, took place at Lost Marsh Golf Club near Wolf Lake, where the Bears would build if they decide to move to Indiana. A statement issued by a team spokesperson said the Bears “continue to work together with Indiana leaders on our commitment to finish the necessary due diligence work for the Hammond site.”</p><p></p><p>In February, Indiana established the Northwest Indiana Stadium Authority, which would issue bonds to finance a stadium. McCaskey said at the NFL’s annual meeting earlier this month that the Bears didn’t yet “have a deal to consider” in Indiana. Due diligence may soon change that.</p><p></p><p>If the Bears moved to Indiana, McCaskey said, the Bears fans would, with time, “get used to it.”</p><p></p><p>Friday’s meeting was a public salvo on the eve of what could be a critical week for the team, which is trying to decide whether to build a domed stadium on the 326 acres it owns in Arlington Heights or move across state lines.</p><p></p><p>The Illinois House of Representatives could vote next week on whether to pass PILOT legislation — shorthand for payment in lieu of taxes — to allow the Bears to renegotiate their property taxes with Arlington Heights. If not, the Bears will have to wait — the House is in session Tuesday through Thursday before returning May 5. The Senate would then have to approve the bill before the General Assembly session closes May 31. Then the Bears would need to negotiate the tax rate with Arlington Heights and receive infrastructure funding.</p><p></p><p>At the NFL annual meeting, Warren, McCaskey and NFL commissioner Roger Goodell preached urgency. The Bears expect to make decision by late spring or early summer.</p><p></p><p>“This is an important time to get this resolved, sooner rather than later,” Goodell said.</p><bsp-list-loadmore title: Bears owner George McCaskey: Legacy, tradition won't stop potential move to Indiana stadium
author: Jason Lieser
summary: <p>PHOENIX — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> fans better wrap their minds around the team moving to Indiana. George McCaskey already has.</p><p>Tradition and legacy are incredibly important to McCaskey, the Bears’ chairman and the grandson of George Halas, and the team has been in his family for more than a century. But as stadium plans in Hammond, Indiana, get increasingly serious, he is at peace with being the one who moves the team out of Illinois and assumes the fan base will move past its initial backlash to the idea.</p><p>“I don’t think, in the end, it’s going to matter to people,” he said Wednesday at the end of the NFL annual meeting. “Back in 1976, the New York Football Giants went across state lines to New Jersey. They have been there ever since. The Jets joined them shortly thereafter. And then 35 years later, both teams had an opportunity to reevaluate their situations and recommitted to New Jersey.</p><p>“And somehow, the Republic has survived.”</p><p>That’s a glib response to fans who were irritated when president Kevin Warren went public last December, leading up to a massive game against the Packers, with the idea of building a stadium in Northwest Indiana.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/04/01/bears-president-kevin-warren-targets-late-spring-or-early-summer-for-stadium-decision" >Bears president Kevin Warren targets late spring or early summer for stadium decision</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/03/31/nfl-commissioner-roger-goodell-bears-need-stadium-solution-soon-arlington-heights-hammond-indiana-annual-meetings" >NFL commissioner Roger Goodell: Bears need to find stadium solution soon</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/halas-intrigue/2026/04/01/bears-stadium-podcast-nfl-annual-meetings-ian-cunningham-rooney-rule-halas-intrigue" >Halas Intrigue podcast: All quiet on the stadium front</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The Bears have played at Soldier Field since 1971, interrupted only by one season at the University of Illinois during renovations, and were at Wrigley Field for 50 years before that. Nearly their entire history has been in Chicago, which made a potential move to the old Arlington Park racetrack site in Arlington Heights a bit hard to accept for some, let alone venturing outside the state.</p><p>Again, if that happens, the Bears’ message is get over it.</p><p>“Whether we go to Arlington Park or to Hammond, there is going to be an adjustment period,” McCaskey said. “People are allowed some time to get used to it. I think Bears fans are up to it.”</p><p>There was no news on the stadium as McCaskey and Warren talked Wednesday morning. There was insight, such as McCaskey’s comments about potentially moving to Indiana and the tension he expressed about his family having to borrow $2 billion to build, but no actual movement.</p><p>That’s a story in itself. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2021/6/17/22538681/bears-arlington-heights-park-bid-plans-chicago" >June will mark five years since the Bears began this process</a> — Matt Nagy and Justin Fields were on the team — and they still can’t even say in which state they’ll build the stadium.</p><p>Warren didn’t express any frustration over the slow pace. He maintained the Bears, despite the delays, are in “an excellent position” with two very appealing options.</p><p>The Bears own a 326-acre property in Arlington Heights and are exploring a 340-acre purchase in Hammond. They have the legislative approval they need in Indiana, but don’t own property there yet. In Illinois, it’s the reverse as they seek tax certainty from the state legislature, which ends its session May 31.</p><p>It’s no coincidence that date lines up with Warren’s remark Wednesday that the organization wants to make a decision by “late spring, early summer.”</p><p>Anything resembling a deadline, of course, is written in pencil.</p><p>It would seem the main reason to stall now rather than proceed toward Indiana is that the Bears would truly prefer to go to Arlington Heights and are giving that as much time as reasonably possible to materialize.</p><p>Warren repeatedly expressed confidence the Bears would get “shovels in the ground” by the end of last year, which would set a timeline for the stadium opening for the 2028 season, but that didn’t happen. Now they’re looking at the 2029 season, and meanwhile the team will continue playing in a building that commissioner Roger Goodell said is “not at the top of the list” in terms of modern amenities and elevated fan experience.</p><p>Perhaps it was incidental, but as McCaskey discussed the stadium options with a small group of Chicago-based reporters, with Warren sitting in the back of the room, he called Arlington Park “shovel-ready.”</p><p>When the Bears hired Warren in 2023 to replace Ted Phillips, his mission was to get them going the right direction on the field, in business and in their pursuit of a new stadium, but the public perception was primarily that he was brought in to get the stadium deal done after he’d been at the forefront of the Vikings’ stadium project.</p><p>The Bears just had their best season in more than a decade, going 11-6 and winning a playoff game — the business is doing fine, too, with a recent Forbes valuation of $8.2 billion — and Warren told the Sun-Times that gives him a little extra fire to accelerate the stadium.</p><p>“And we will,” he said firmly. “That is the dream, to have a world-class team playing in a world-class stadium.”</p><p>If that happens in Indiana, so be it.</p><p>It certainly wasn’t Plan A and still might not be. But the Bears — and, most importantly, McCaskey — are comfortable with it.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" title: Bears president Kevin Warren targets late spring or early summer for stadium decision
author: Jason Lieser
summary: <p>PHOENIX — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> president Kevin Warren said Wednesday the organization is in an "excellent position" as it seeks to build a new stadium in Arlington Heights or Hammond, Ind. despite being nearly five years into the process and still being unsettled on the location.</p><p>"One good thing about it: Both of the sites are excellent sites," Warren said in a small media gathering at the end of the NFL's annual meeting. "We're focused on making sure we build a world-class stadium."</p><p>Warren said he intends to finalize the decision by "late spring [or] early summer." If the Bears break ground on a stadium this year, it would be on a timeline to open for the 2029 season. They'll continue playing at Soldier Field in the meantime, and their lease runs through the 2033 season.</p><p>The Bears <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2021/9/28/22689110/bears-arlington-racecourse-height-soldier-field-lori-lightfoot-george-mccaskey-move-relocate-chicago" >began the process of building a new stadium in 2021</a> when they moved to acquire the 326-acre Arlington Park racetrack property. They hired Warren in January 2023 to replace longtime president Ted Phillips.</p>

title: NFL commissioner Roger Goodell: Bears need to find stadium solution soon
author: Patrick Finley
summary: <p>PHOENIX — Whether the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> decide to build a stadium in Arlington Heights or Hammond, Indiana, Roger Goodell believes the time has come for them to work out a deal.</p><p>“They need to find a solution for a stadium,” Goodell said Tuesday at his NFL Annual Meeting press conference. "They have looked not only in Indiana but also in Illinois at other sites, and invested in a site. I think they have been responsible in that fact.</p><p>“I think it’s really important that they come to a resolution on this relatively soon. … This is an important time to get this resolved.”</p><p>Bears chairman George McCaskey and president/CEO Kevin Warren figure to stress a similar urgency when they meet with the media Wednesday at the Arizona Biltmore. The Bears are seeking property tax cuts on the 326 acres they own in Arlington Heights and want the Illinois General Assembly to allow them to negotiate a payment-in-lieu-of-taxes. The assembly is in session through May 31, leaving just two months to work out an agreement.</p><p>Indiana looms. In late February, the state of Indiana <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/02/26/bears-stadium-hammond-indiana-hammong-senate-passes-bill-27-arlington-heights-george-mccaaskey-kevin-warren-nfl" target="_blank" >passed a bill</a> that established the Northwest Indiana Stadium Authority, which provided the vehicle to finance a Bears stadium in Hammond.</p><p>Goodell has toured stadium sites in both states and said he’s spoken recently with officials from Illinois.</p><p>Asked directly by the Sun-Times if he believed the Bears should play their home games in a different state, Goodell said the team was “looking at the best resolution,” wherever it may be.</p><p>“That’s an important element, as you know, to the success of a founding team,” he said.</p><p>Soldier Field has great tradition, he said, but lacks advancements in technology that contributes to the overall fan experience.</p><p>Goodell addressed other issues Tuesday afternoon, saying the NFL’s Rooney Rule, which aims to encourage diversity of hiring candidates, isn’t going anywhere despite threats of legal action in Florida.</p><p>Goodell said negotiations haven’t progressed as far as he’d hoped with the NFL Referees Association. The two sides are staring down a work stoppage at the end of May. The NFL passed a rule Tuesday that allows the league to use replay to fix obvious officiating mistakes if a game is being called by replacement referees this season.</p><p>Other rule changes passed Tuesday allow teams to declare an onside kick at any point during the game. The kicking team no longer has an incentive to kick the ball out of bounds when they kick off from the 50 after a penalty. The kick return team can now align slightly differently.</p><p>Goodell said there was no talk of changing the free agency legal tampering period in the wake of Maxx Crosby’s failed physical. He also said he expects NFL players to participate in flag football at the 2028 Olympics.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" title: With Bears in mind, Sanders bill would offer up sports teams to city before 'billionaire owners' try to move
author: Tina Sfondeles
summary: <p>Sen. Bernie Sanders and Texas Rep. Greg Casar want communities to be able to buy a sports team before "billionaire owners" try to move it, very pointedly bashing the Chicago Bears' effort to relocate to Indiana which Casar repeatedly likened to "negotiating with a gun" to the head.</p><p>While it's typically never a good thing for the Chicago Bears to be compared to the Green Bay Packers, a new bill would allow the Bears, and any other sports team, to be offered up for sale one year before sports team owners can move it to another state or metropolitan area. The legislation would lift a prohibition on teams being publicly owned, like the Packers are. The Wisconsin team is a non profit franchise in the NFL, with more than 538,000 shareholders. </p><p>Casar even went so far to say that "this is a keep-the-Bears-in-Chicago bill" during a Washington press conference on Thursday. </p><p>The Home Team Act would require an owner to announce that it wants to relocate a year prior, giving the community, not-for-profits or private investors a chance to buy it at "fair market value," including through the community ownership model of the Packers. Franchise owners would be penalized if they don't comply with the one-year notice.</p><p>"There is a right of first refusal to the local community, to community nonprofits and partnerships and for ultimately, if it's just a wealthy family that wants to keep it, they get a shot at it, too," Casar said. "But you could imagine a world where the city has a stake in the team, alongside other partners."</p><p>If no one wants to buy the team and keep it in the home city, owners can then move it. Casara called it a way for fans and taxpayers to "finally get a fair deal."</p><p>"Even when teams don't actually move, the threat of moving sets off a race to the bottom. Billionaire owners pit taxpayers against one another and then extort the government for billions of dollars," Casar said.</p><p>"We see that right now in Chicago, where Indiana taxpayers are now put in a competition against Illinois taxpayers to subsidize a team worth $8 billion," he said. "Before you move a team away from the fans who have been rooting for it their whole life, you have to give them a chance to buy it and keep it."</p><p>Casar said it's possible to get "much better deals if you aren't negotiating with a gun to your head, like we're seeing right now in Illinois." </p><p>Sanders said the departure of the Dodgers from Brooklyn, New York had a very negative impact on the state, and he called the new legislation "emotional."</p><p>"It's a big deal, and we should not let the greed of a handful of billionaires make it hard for working-class families to enjoy their local teams," Sanders said.</p><p>Indiana state legislators last month advanced legislation <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/02/19/chicago-bears-stadium-hammond-indiana-move" target="_blank" >creating a stadium finance authority that would help the Bears build a dome in Hammond</a>, a move that the team called "the most meaningful step forward" in a dramatic saga that has stretched on for more than three years. It was also a step taken by the Bears that frustrated Illinois officials, who are trying to craft a deal to keep the Bears in Arlington Heights, a destination that Gov. JB Pritzker and other Illinois Democrats say remains within reach. </p><p>A partial plan to help the NFL franchise move to Arlington Heights moved out of an Illinois House committee in late February. But its <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/02/26/chicago-bears-property-tax-incentives-illinois-house-city-opposition-arlington-heights-proposed-stadium" target="_blank" >legislative prospects are in question</a> after City Hall withheld support and kept pushing for at least $630 million in infrastructure and Soldier Field renovation concessions.</p>

title: Chicago Fire breaks ground on $750 million stadium at The 78
author: Abby Miller
summary: <p>The Chicago Fire broke ground Tuesday on a $750 million soccer stadium in the South Loop, which was also a first step toward developing the long-dormant parcel known as The 78.</p><p>The 22,000-seat stadium, bankrolled by the Fire’s billionaire owner, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/06/03/chicago-fire-soccer-stadium-south-loop-the-78-joe-mansueto-related-midwest" >Joe Mansueto</a>, is expected to be complete in time for the team’s 2028-29 season. The soccer stadium will be a huge boon for the team, which currently plays at Soldier Field but has had games pushed to the suburbs due to scheduling conflicts with the Chicago Bears and concerts.</p><p>“This is a culmination of some work that seeks to turn some of the most valuable and prominent pieces of fallow land in the city of Chicago into a world-class stadium and a vibrant surrounding community,” Ald. Pat Dowell (3rd), whose ward includes the project, said.</p><p>The stadium will serve as an anchor for The 78, the 62-acre site at Roosevelt Road and Clark Street that has eluded development for years. The land, owned by Related Midwest, is one of the largest undeveloped parcels left in the city.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fire/2025/09/18/chicago-fire-stadium-the78-plan-commission-approvals" >first phase</a> of development at The 78 will include more than 1,400 feet of publicly-accessible riverfront space, a new water taxi stop, 1 1/2 miles of bike trails, Divvy bike stations, two temporary surface parking lots, public parking and 3 acres of sports fields, according to Related Midwest.</p><p>Once the 62-acre project is complete, it's estimated to generate $8 billion in economic impact. The development will also include homes, trails and a connection to Ping Tom Memorial Park.</p><p>“This not only will be a great place to come watch a soccer match or concert, it'll be a fantastic place to call home for thousands of Chicagoans,” Dave Baldwin, Chicago Fire’s president of business operations, said.</p><p>Mansueto had two options when selecting the team's permanent home: The 78 and the now-defunct Lincoln Yards megadevelopment. Lincoln Yards collapsed last year and a large portion of the North Side project was purchased by Chicago-based JDL Development, who received the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/02/18/chicago-city-council-foundry-park-successor-failed-lincoln-yards-project-north-side" >City Council’s approval</a> last month for a scaled-back
